A horizontal force of $24\;\mathrm{N}$ pushes on the $1.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block. Find the magnitude of the contact force between the $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ blocks, in newtons.
solution: The system accelerates at $a = 24/6.0 = 4.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The contact force in question is the only horizontal force on the $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block, so it equals $(3.0)(4.0) = 12\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Pushing downward at an angle
statement: A worker pushes a $15\;\mathrm{kg}$ crate along a frictionless floor with a $100\;\mathrm{N}$ force directed $20^\circ$ below the horizontal. Find the normal force from the floor, in newtons.
solution: Vertically, the floor must support the weight plus the downward component of the push: $N = mg + F\sin 20^\circ = 147 + 34.2 = 181\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Bird accelerating upward
statement: A $0.25\;\mathrm{kg}$ bird accelerates straight upward at $3.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the upward force the air exerts on the bird, in newtons.
solution: Two forces act: gravity down and the air force up. So $F - mg = ma$ and $F = m(g+a) = 0.25(12.8) = 3.2\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Braking car
statement: A $1200\;\mathrm{kg}$ car traveling at $25\;\mathrm{m/s}$ is brought to rest in $4.0\;\mathrm{s}$. Find the magnitude of the average net force on the car, in newtons.
solution: The average acceleration is $a = 25/4.0 = 6.25\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Then $F = ma = (1200)(6.25) = 7500\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Ball bouncing off a wall
statement: A $0.15\;\mathrm{kg}$ ball strikes a wall at $20\;\mathrm{m/s}$ and rebounds straight back at $15\;\mathrm{m/s}$. The contact lasts $0.020\;\mathrm{s}$. Find the magnitude of the average force the wall exerts on the ball, in newtons.
solution: The velocity changes by $35\;\mathrm{m/s}$ because the direction reverses. So $F = m\Delta v/\Delta t = (0.15)(35)/0.020 = 262\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Accelerometer on a string
statement: A small ball hangs from a string tied to the ceiling of a car. While the car accelerates in a straight line the string hangs at a steady $12^\circ$ from the vertical. Find the magnitude of the car's acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The string tension has a vertical component balancing gravity, $T\cos\theta = mg$, and a horizontal component providing the acceleration, $T\sin\theta = ma$. Dividing gives $a = g\tan 12^\circ = 2.08\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Astronaut pushes a capsule
statement: A $60\;\mathrm{kg}$ astronaut floating in space pushes off a $120\;\mathrm{kg}$ capsule, giving the capsule an acceleration of $0.40\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the magnitude of the astronaut's acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: By the third law the two forces have equal magnitude: $F = (120)(0.40) = 48\;\mathrm{N}$. The astronaut's acceleration is then $48/60 = 0.80\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Holding a block on a frictionless incline
statement: An $8.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block rests on a frictionless incline of angle $20^\circ$. It is held in place by a horizontal push. Find the magnitude of that push, in newtons.
solution: Resolve along and perpendicular to the incline, or use the closed force triangle of weight, normal force and horizontal push. Either way $F = mg\tan\theta = (8.0)(9.8)\tan 20^\circ = 28.5\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Accelerating wedge
statement: A block rests on the frictionless $25^\circ$ face of a wedge. The wedge is pushed horizontally so that the block stays in the same spot on the face, not sliding at all. Find the required acceleration of the wedge, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Only two forces act on the block: gravity and the normal force. Their sum must be horizontal and equal to $ma$. Vertically $N\cos\theta = mg$ and horizontally $N\sin\theta = ma$, so $a = g\tan 25^\circ = 4.57\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Cables at two angles
statement: A $25\;\mathrm{kg}$ traffic light hangs from two cables attached to the same point. One cable rises at $40^\circ$ above the horizontal to the left, the other at $50^\circ$ above the horizontal to the right. Find the tension in the $40^\circ$ cable, in newtons.
solution: Horizontal balance gives $T_1\cos 40^\circ = T_2\cos 50^\circ$ and vertical balance gives $T_1\sin 40^\circ + T_2\sin 50^\circ = mg$. Because the cables are perpendicular, the algebra collapses to $T_1 = mg\cos 50^\circ = 245(0.643) = 157\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Friction on a stacked block
statement: A $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block sits on top of a $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block, which rests on a frictionless floor. A horizontal force of $21\;\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the lower block, and the two move together. Find the friction force acting on the upper block, in newtons.
solution: Together they accelerate at $a = 21/7.0 = 3.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Friction from the lower block is the only horizontal force on the upper block, so $f = (2.0)(3.0) = 6.0\;\mathrm{N}$ in the direction of motion.

name: Tension inside a hanging chain
statement: A uniform chain of mass $6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ hangs at rest from a hook. Find the tension in the chain at a point one third of the way up from the bottom, in newtons.
solution: Cut the chain at that point and draw a free body diagram of the piece below it. That piece has mass $(1/3)(6.0) = 2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and is in equilibrium, so the tension supports its weight: $T = (2.0)(9.8) = 19.6\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Tension in a massive rope
statement: A $10\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hangs from a uniform rope of mass $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$. The rope is pulled straight up so the whole system accelerates upward at $2.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the tension at the midpoint of the rope, in newtons.
solution: Everything below the midpoint has mass $10 + 2.0 = 12\;\mathrm{kg}$. For that piece, $T - mg = ma$, so $T = 12(9.8+2.0) = 142\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Pushing a rope along the floor
statement: A uniform rope of mass $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and length $3.0\;\mathrm{m}$ lies on a frictionless floor. It is pushed along its length by a $12\;\mathrm{N}$ force applied to one end. Find the magnitude of the internal force in the rope at a point $1.0\;\mathrm{m}$ from the pushed end, in newtons.
solution: The rope accelerates at $a = 12/5.0 = 2.4\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The section ahead of the cut has mass $(2.0/3.0)(5.0) = 3.33\;\mathrm{kg}$, and the internal force is what accelerates it: $F = (3.33)(2.4) = 8.0\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Block on a free wedge
statement: A $1.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block slides on the frictionless $30^\circ$ face of a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ wedge, and the wedge itself is free to slide on a frictionless floor. Find the magnitude of the wedge's acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The horizontal push on the wedge comes only from the normal force, and the block's motion is constrained to stay on the moving face. Solving the coupled equations gives $A = \frac{mg\sin\theta\cos\theta}{M+m\sin^2\theta}$. With the numbers, $A = 4.243/3.25 = 1.31\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Painter on a hanging platform
statement: A $60\;\mathrm{kg}$ painter stands on a $15\;\mathrm{kg}$ platform. A rope attached to the platform runs up over a frictionless pulley and back down to the painter's hands. He pulls so that he and the platform accelerate upward at $0.80\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the force the platform exerts on the painter, in newtons.
solution: Two rope segments hold the system up, so for painter plus platform, $2T - (75)(9.8) = 75(0.80)$, giving $T = 397.5\;\mathrm{N}$. Now take the painter alone: $N + T - m_pg = m_pa$, so $N = 60(10.6) - 397.5 = 238\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Kinetic friction on a sliding crate
statement: A $12\;\mathrm{kg}$ crate slides across a level floor with $\mu_k = 0.35$. Find the kinetic friction force on the crate, in newtons.
solution: On a level floor $N = mg = 117.6\;\mathrm{N}$. Then $f_k = \mu_k N = (0.35)(117.6) = 41.2\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Maximum static friction
statement: An $8.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ toolbox sits on a level bench with $\mu_s = 0.45$. Find the largest static friction force the bench can supply, in newtons.
solution: The maximum is $f_{s,max} = \mu_s N = \mu_s mg = (0.45)(8.0)(9.8) = 35.3\;\mathrm{N}$. Static friction can be anything from zero up to this value.

name: Acceleration against friction
statement: A $10\;\mathrm{kg}$ box is pushed horizontally with $25\;\mathrm{N}$ across a floor with $\mu_k = 0.20$. Find the box's acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Friction opposes the push: $f_k = (0.20)(10)(9.8) = 19.6\;\mathrm{N}$. Then $a = (25-19.6)/10 = 0.54\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Skid distance
statement: A car traveling at $20\;\mathrm{m/s}$ locks its brakes on a level road with $\mu_k = 0.70$. Find the distance it skids before stopping, in meters.
solution: The deceleration is $a = \mu_k g = 6.86\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, independent of mass. Then $d = v^2/(2a) = 400/13.72 = 29.2\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Coefficient from deceleration
statement: A block sliding on a level table slows down at $2.5\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the coefficient of kinetic friction between block and table.
solution: Friction is the only horizontal force, so $\mu_k mg = ma$ and $\mu_k = a/g = 2.5/9.8 = 0.255$.

name: Angle of repose
statement: A ramp is slowly tilted until a block placed on it just begins to slide, which happens at $32^\circ$. Find the coefficient of static friction.
solution: At the tipping point $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, so $\mu_s = \tan\theta = \tan 32^\circ = 0.625$.

name: Steepest ramp that holds
statement: A carton has $\mu_s = 0.60$ against a wooden ramp. Find the steepest ramp angle on which the carton will not slide, in degrees.
solution: The critical angle satisfies $\tan\theta = \mu_s$, so $\theta = \arctan 0.60 = 31.0^\circ$.

name: Force to start a crate moving
statement: A $50\;\mathrm{kg}$ crate rests on a level floor with $\mu_s = 0.40$. Find the minimum horizontal force needed to start it moving, in newtons.
solution: The push must exceed the maximum static friction, $\mu_s mg = (0.40)(50)(9.8) = 196\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Puck on ice
statement: A hockey puck launched at $12\;\mathrm{m/s}$ slides $40\;\mathrm{m}$ before stopping. Find the coefficient of kinetic friction between puck and ice.
solution: The deceleration is $a = v^2/(2d) = 144/80 = 1.8\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $\mu_k = a/g = 1.8/9.8 = 0.184$.

name: Sliding down a rough incline
statement: A block slides down a $20^\circ$ incline with $\mu_k = 0.25$. Find the magnitude of its acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Along the incline, $ma = mg\sin\theta - \mu_k mg\cos\theta$, so $a = g(\sin 20^\circ - 0.25\cos 20^\circ) = 9.8(0.342-0.235) = 1.05\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Static friction is not always maximal
statement: A $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block sits at rest on a $30^\circ$ incline with $\mu_s = 0.70$. Find the friction force acting on the block, in newtons.
solution: First check whether it slips: the pull along the incline is $mg\sin 30^\circ = 24.5\;\mathrm{N}$, while the maximum friction is $\mu_s mg\cos 30^\circ = 29.7\;\mathrm{N}$. It holds, so friction takes exactly the value needed for equilibrium, $24.5\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Block sent up a rough incline
statement: A $6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block is launched up a $25^\circ$ incline with $\mu_k = 0.30$. Find the magnitude of its deceleration while moving up, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Going up, gravity and friction both act down the slope: $a = g(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta) = 9.8(0.423+0.272) = 6.81\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Dragging with an angled rope
statement: A $20\;\mathrm{kg}$ trunk is dragged at constant speed across a floor with $\mu_k = 0.30$ by a rope at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. Find the rope tension, in newtons.
solution: Lifting at an angle reduces the normal force: $N = mg - T\sin\theta$. Constant speed means $T\cos\theta = \mu_k N$, so $T = \mu_k mg/(\cos\theta + \mu_k\sin\theta) = 58.8/1.016 = 57.9\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Pushing a stack without slipping
statement: A $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block rests on a $7.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless floor, with $\mu_s = 0.40$ between the blocks. A horizontal force is applied to the lower block. Find the largest force for which the blocks still move together, in newtons.
solution: Friction is the only horizontal force on the upper block, so its maximum acceleration is $a_{max} = \mu_s g = 3.92\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Driving the whole $10\;\mathrm{kg}$ at that rate needs $F = (10)(3.92) = 39.2\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Cargo in a braking truck
statement: A crate sits on the flat bed of a truck with $\mu_s = 0.50$ between crate and bed. Find the largest deceleration the truck can have without the crate sliding forward, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Friction must supply the crate's deceleration, and it can supply at most $\mu_s mg$. So $a_{max} = \mu_s g = 4.9\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, independent of the crate's mass.

name: Box dropped on a conveyor belt
statement: A box is placed at rest on a conveyor belt that moves at a steady $4.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$. The coefficient of kinetic friction is $0.25$. Find how far the box slips relative to the belt before matching its speed, in meters.
solution: The box accelerates at $\mu_k g = 2.45\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and reaches $4.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$ after $t = 1.633\;\mathrm{s}$. In that time the belt moves $6.53\;\mathrm{m}$ and the box $3.27\;\mathrm{m}$, so the slip is $3.27\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Fastest safe speed on a flat curve
statement: A car rounds a flat, unbanked curve of radius $80\;\mathrm{m}$ on a road with $\mu_s = 0.60$. Find the maximum speed it can have, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Friction supplies the centripetal force: $\mu_s mg = mv^2/r$. So $v = \sqrt{\mu_s gr} = \sqrt{(0.60)(9.8)(80)} = 21.7\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Heavy crate on a rope
statement: A $100\;\mathrm{kg}$ crate is pulled at constant speed by a rope $20^\circ$ above the horizontal across a floor with $\mu_k = 0.40$. Find the rope tension, in newtons.
solution: With $N = mg - T\sin\theta$ and $T\cos\theta = \mu_k N$, we get $T = \mu_k mg/(\cos\theta + \mu_k\sin\theta) = 392/1.0765 = 364\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: How far up the ramp
statement: A block is launched up a $30^\circ$ incline at $8.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$ with $\mu_k = 0.20$. Find how far along the incline it travels before stopping, in meters.
solution: The deceleration is $g(\sin 30^\circ + 0.20\cos 30^\circ) = 6.60\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Then $d = v^2/(2a) = 64/13.19 = 4.85\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Return speed down the ramp
statement: The block of the previous setup ($30^\circ$ incline, launched at $8.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$, $\mu_k = \mu_s = 0.20$) slides back down. Find its speed when it returns to the starting point, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Since $\mu_s < \tan 30^\circ$ the block does slide back. Coming down the acceleration is $g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta) = 3.20\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$ over the same $4.85\;\mathrm{m}$, giving $v = \sqrt{2(3.20)(4.85)} = 5.57\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Block held against a wall
statement: A $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ book is held against a vertical wall by a horizontal push. The coefficient of static friction is $0.50$. Find the minimum push needed to keep the book from sliding down, in newtons.
solution: The push sets the normal force, and friction acts vertically: $\mu_s F \ge mg$. So $F_{min} = mg/\mu_s = 39.2/0.50 = 78.4\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Steady haul up a slope
statement: A $10\;\mathrm{kg}$ box is pulled up a $30^\circ$ incline at constant speed by a force parallel to the incline, with $\mu_k = 0.15$. Find the required force, in newtons.
solution: Constant speed means the applied force balances gravity's component plus friction: $F = mg(\sin\theta + \mu_k\cos\theta) = 98(0.5+0.130) = 61.7\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Which surface gives way first
statement: A $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block sits on a $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block that rests on the ground. The coefficient of static friction is $0.30$ between the blocks and $0.20$ between the lower block and the ground. A horizontal force is applied to the upper block. Find the largest force for which nothing moves, in newtons.
solution: Check both interfaces. The ground can resist up to $(0.20)(6.0)(9.8) = 11.8\;\mathrm{N}$, but the upper block can only be held by $(0.30)(2.0)(9.8) = 5.88\;\mathrm{N}$. The weaker interface gives way first, so motion begins once $F$ exceeds $5.88\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Ladder against a smooth wall
statement: A uniform ladder leans against a frictionless vertical wall, with $\mu_s = 0.40$ at the floor. Find the smallest angle between the ladder and the floor for which it does not slip, in degrees.
solution: Force balance gives $N_{floor} = W$ and $f = N_{wall}$. Taking torques about the base, $N_{wall}L\sin\theta = W(L/2)\cos\theta$, so $N_{wall} = W/(2\tan\theta)$. Requiring $N_{wall} \le \mu_s W$ gives $\tan\theta \ge 1/(2\mu_s) = 1.25$, so $\theta_{min} = 51.3^\circ$.

name: Horizontal force holding a block on a slope
statement: A $10\;\mathrm{kg}$ block sits on a $40^\circ$ incline with $\mu_s = 0.30$, which is not enough to hold it. A horizontal force is applied, pressing toward the incline. Find the minimum such force that keeps the block from sliding down, in newtons.
solution: The horizontal push both helps along the slope and increases the normal force. With $N = mg\cos\theta + F\sin\theta$ and $mg\sin\theta = F\cos\theta + \mu_s N$ at the verge of slipping, $F = mg(\sin\theta-\mu_s\cos\theta)/(\cos\theta+\mu_s\sin\theta) = 40.5/0.959 = 42.2\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Two blocks with different friction
statement: A $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block ($\mu_k = 0.10$) is connected by a taut string to a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block ($\mu_k = 0.40$) directly behind it, and the pair slides down a $30^\circ$ incline with the lighter block leading. Find the tension in the string, in newtons.
solution: The slippier block would accelerate faster alone, so the string goes taut and they share one acceleration $a = g(\sin\theta - \bar\mu\cos\theta)$ with $\bar\mu = 0.28$. Writing the equation for either block gives $T = \frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}g\cos\theta(\mu_2-\mu_1) = 3.06\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Best angle to pull
statement: A $25\;\mathrm{kg}$ sled is dragged at constant speed over ground with $\mu_k = 0.50$. The rope angle can be chosen freely. Find the smallest possible rope tension, in newtons.
solution: For a rope at angle $\theta$, $T = \mu_k mg/(\cos\theta + \mu_k\sin\theta)$. The denominator is largest when $\tan\theta = \mu_k$, where it equals $\sqrt{1+\mu_k^2}$. So $T_{min} = \mu_k mg/\sqrt{1+\mu_k^2} = 122.5/1.118 = 110\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Ramp then floor
statement: A block slides from rest down $3.0\;\mathrm{m}$ along a $30^\circ$ incline with $\mu_k = 0.20$, then continues onto a horizontal floor with $\mu_k = 0.35$. Find how far it travels on the floor before stopping, in meters.
solution: On the ramp $a = g(\sin 30^\circ - 0.20\cos 30^\circ) = 3.20\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, so $v^2 = 2(3.20)(3.0) = 19.2\;\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$ at the bottom. On the floor the deceleration is $\mu_k g = 3.43\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, giving $d = 19.2/6.86 = 2.80\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Friction needed on an accelerating ramp
statement: A block rides on the $20^\circ$ face of a wedge while the wedge is driven horizontally at $3.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, in the direction that pushes the block into the hill. Find the minimum coefficient of static friction that keeps the block from sliding on the face.
solution: Work in the wedge frame, adding a pseudo-force $ma$ opposite the acceleration. Along the surface the block needs $f = m(g\sin\theta - a\cos\theta)$, and perpendicular $N = m(g\cos\theta + a\sin\theta)$. Then $\mu_{min} = f/N = 0.533/10.23 = 0.052$: the acceleration does most of the work of holding the block.

name: Stack that does slip
statement: A $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block sits on a $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless floor, with $\mu_s = \mu_k = 0.40$ between them. A horizontal force of $40\;\mathrm{N}$ is applied to the lower block. Find the acceleration of the lower block, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: First test whether they move together: that would need $a = 40/7.0 = 5.71\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, but friction can only give the top block $\mu_s g = 3.92\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. So it slips, and the lower block feels $40\;\mathrm{N}$ forward minus kinetic friction $7.84\;\mathrm{N}$ backward: $a = 32.16/5.0 = 6.43\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Hanging mass
statement: A $6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ sandbag hangs at rest from a rope. Find the tension in the rope, in newtons.
solution: At rest the tension balances the weight: $T = mg = (6.0)(9.8) = 58.8\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Atwood machine acceleration
statement: Masses of $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ hang from opposite ends of a light string over a frictionless pulley. Find the magnitude of their acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Treat the pair as one system driven by the weight difference: $a = (m_2-m_1)g/(m_1+m_2) = (2.0)(9.8)/8.0 = 2.45\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Atwood machine tension
statement: For the same Atwood machine ($3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$, frictionless pulley), find the string tension, in newtons.
solution: Apply the second law to the light mass: $T - m_1g = m_1a$, giving $T = 3.0(9.8+2.45) = 36.75\;\mathrm{N}$. Equivalently $T = 2m_1m_2g/(m_1+m_2)$.

name: Elevator cable
statement: An $800\;\mathrm{kg}$ elevator car accelerates upward at $1.2\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the tension in its cable, in newtons.

name: Table and hanging block
statement: A $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless table is connected by a string over a pulley at the table edge to a $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hanging freely. Find the acceleration of the system, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Only the hanging weight drives the $6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ system: $a = m_2g/(m_1+m_2) = 19.6/6.0 = 3.27\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Tension in that string
statement: For the setup above ($4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ on a frictionless table, $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ hanging), find the string tension, in newtons.
solution: The tension is the only horizontal force on the table block: $T = m_1a = (4.0)(3.267) = 13.1\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Two blocks pulled by a string
statement: A $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block and a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block are joined by a light string on a frictionless floor. A $25\;\mathrm{N}$ horizontal force pulls the $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block. Find the string tension, in newtons.
solution: The system accelerates at $25/5.0 = 5.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and the string alone pulls the $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block: $T = (2.0)(5.0) = 10\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Sign on two wires
statement: A $15\;\mathrm{kg}$ sign hangs from two identical vertical wires that share the load equally. Find the tension in each wire, in newtons.
solution: The two tensions together support the weight: $2T = mg$, so $T = 147/2 = 73.5\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Balanced pulley
statement: Two $10\;\mathrm{kg}$ masses hang from opposite ends of a rope over a frictionless pulley. Find the rope tension, in newtons.
solution: Equal masses mean no acceleration, so each side is in equilibrium and $T = mg = 98\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Climber sliding down a rope
statement: A $65\;\mathrm{kg}$ climber slides down a rope while accelerating downward at $1.5\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the tension in the rope, in newtons.
solution: With down as the direction of acceleration, $mg - T = ma$, so $T = m(g-a) = 65(8.3) = 540\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Movable pulley advantage
statement: A $40\;\mathrm{kg}$ load hangs from a movable pulley supported by two parallel segments of the same rope. The load is raised slowly at constant speed. Find the force needed on the free end, in newtons.
solution: Both rope segments have the same tension and together support the load: $2T = mg$. So $T = 392/2 = 196\;\mathrm{N}$, half the weight (at the cost of pulling twice the length of rope).

name: Three blocks in a train
statement: Blocks of $1.0\;\mathrm{kg}$, $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ are connected in that order by light strings on a frictionless floor, and an $18\;\mathrm{N}$ force pulls the $1.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block. Find the tension in the string between the $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ blocks, in newtons.
solution: The train accelerates at $18/6.0 = 3.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The last string pulls only the $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block, so $T = (3.0)(3.0) = 9.0\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Pulley with friction on the table
statement: A $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a table ($\mu_k = 0.20$) is connected over a frictionless pulley to a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ hanging block. Find the acceleration of the system, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The driving force is the hanging weight $29.4\;\mathrm{N}$ minus friction $\mu_k m_1g = 9.8\;\mathrm{N}$. Then $a = 19.6/8.0 = 2.45\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Force on the pulley axle
statement: For an Atwood machine with $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$, find the total downward force the rope exerts on the pulley axle, in newtons.
solution: Both rope segments hang vertically and each pulls down with the same tension $36.75\;\mathrm{N}$, so the axle feels $2T = 73.5\;\mathrm{N}$. Note this is less than the combined weight of $78.4\;\mathrm{N}$, because the system is accelerating.

name: Constraint in a block and tackle
statement: In a block and tackle, a load hangs from a movable pulley supported by two rope segments, and the free end is pulled at $1.2\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the speed at which the load rises, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Shortening each of the two supporting segments by $x$ takes $2x$ of rope through your hands, so the load moves half as fast as the free end: $v = 1.2/2 = 0.60\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Incline and hanging mass
statement: A $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block rests on a frictionless $30^\circ$ incline and is joined by a string over a pulley at the top to a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hanging vertically. Find the acceleration of the system, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The hanging weight $29.4\;\mathrm{N}$ competes with the incline component $mg\sin 30^\circ = 19.6\;\mathrm{N}$. So $a = 9.8/7.0 = 1.4\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, with the hanging block descending.

name: Tension for the incline system
statement: For the previous setup ($4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ on a frictionless $30^\circ$ incline, $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ hanging), find the string tension, in newtons.
solution: Apply the second law to the hanging block: $m_2g - T = m_2a$, so $T = 3.0(9.8-1.4) = 25.2\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Lower string in a hanging pair
statement: A $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hangs from a string, and a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hangs from the bottom of the $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block by a second string. The whole assembly is hauled upward at $2.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the tension in the lower string, in newtons.
solution: The lower string supports only the $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block: $T = m(g+a) = 3.0(11.8) = 35.4\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Upper string in the same pair
statement: For the same assembly ($5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ above, $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ below, hauled upward at $2.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$), find the tension in the upper string, in newtons.
solution: The upper string carries everything below it, a total of $8.0\;\mathrm{kg}$: $T = 8.0(11.8) = 94.4\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Rope with mass
statement: An $8.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hangs from a uniform rope of mass $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$. The top of the rope is pulled upward so the system accelerates upward at $1.5\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the tension at the top of the rope, in newtons.
solution: At the top the rope must accelerate everything below it, $10\;\mathrm{kg}$ in all: $T = 10(11.3) = 113\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Rope strength limit
statement: A $12\;\mathrm{kg}$ bucket is hoisted from a well by a rope that will break at $200\;\mathrm{N}$. Find the greatest upward acceleration that can be used, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Distance fallen on an Atwood machine
statement: An Atwood machine carries $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and $6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and is released from rest. Find how far the heavier mass falls in $2.0\;\mathrm{s}$, in meters.
solution: The acceleration is $a = (2.0)(9.8)/10 = 1.96\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, constant. Then $d = \tfrac12at^2 = \tfrac12(1.96)(4.0) = 3.92\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Movable pulley with a counterweight
statement: One end of a rope is attached to an $8.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hanging freely. The rope runs up over a fixed pulley, down around a movable pulley carrying a $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ load, and its other end is tied to the ceiling. Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ load, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The movable pulley moves half as fast as the rope end, so $a_8 = 2a_5$. Its equations are $2T - m_5g = m_5a_5$ and $m_8g - T = m_8(2a_5)$. Eliminating $T$: $a_5 = (2m_8-m_5)g/(m_5+4m_8) = 107.8/37 = 2.91\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$ upward.

name: Stacked masses on an Atwood machine
statement: An Atwood machine has a $6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on one side. On the other side a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hangs from the string, and a $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hangs beneath it from a short cord. Find the tension in that short cord, in newtons.
solution: The system accelerates at $a = (6.0-5.0)(9.8)/11 = 0.891\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, with the lighter side rising. The short cord holds only the $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block, which accelerates upward: $T = 2.0(9.8+0.891) = 21.4\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Monkey and counterweight
statement: A $20\;\mathrm{kg}$ monkey grips a rope that passes over a frictionless pulley and holds a $25\;\mathrm{kg}$ counterweight on the other side. The monkey climbs so that it accelerates upward at $1.2\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$ relative to the ground. Find the magnitude of the counterweight's acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: For the monkey, $T - m g = m a$ gives $T = 20(11.0) = 220\;\mathrm{N}$. The same tension acts on the counterweight: $25(9.8) - 220 = 25a$, so $a = 1.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$ downward.

name: Two inclines and a pulley
statement: A $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless $30^\circ$ incline is connected over a pulley at the apex to a $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless $45^\circ$ incline on the other side. Find the magnitude of the acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Each block feels $mg\sin\theta$ along its own face. The net driving force is $5(9.8)\sin 45^\circ - 4(9.8)\sin 30^\circ = 34.65-19.6 = 15.05\;\mathrm{N}$ on a total of $9.0\;\mathrm{kg}$, so $a = 1.67\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Rope around a movable pulley on a table
statement: A $10\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless table has a rope tied to it. The rope runs horizontally to the table edge, down around a movable pulley carrying a $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ load, then back up to a fixed anchor. Find the acceleration of the $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ load, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The load hangs on two rope segments, so it moves half as fast as the block: $a_{block} = 2a_{load}$. With $T = m_b a_{block}$ and $m_\ell g - 2T = m_\ell a_{load}$, we get $39.2 = 2(10)(2a_\ell) + 4a_\ell = 44a_\ell$, so $a_\ell = 0.891\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Partway up a massive rope
statement: A $7.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hangs from a uniform rope of mass $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$, and the whole thing is accelerated upward at $2.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the tension at the point one quarter of the way up the rope from the block, in newtons.
solution: Cut the rope there; below the cut is the block plus a quarter of the rope, $7.0+0.75 = 7.75\;\mathrm{kg}$. Then $T = 7.75(11.8) = 91.5\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Atwood machine inside an elevator
statement: An Atwood machine with $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ and $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ hangs from the ceiling of an elevator that accelerates upward at $2.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the string tension, in newtons.
solution: In the elevator frame the pseudo-force acts like extra gravity, so replace $g$ with $g_{eff} = 9.8+2.0 = 11.8\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Then $T = 2m_1m_2g_{eff}/(m_1+m_2) = 2(6)(11.8)/5 = 28.3\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Climbing monkey, equal counterweight
statement: A $15\;\mathrm{kg}$ monkey hangs from a rope over a frictionless pulley, with a $15\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on the other end. The monkey climbs with an acceleration of $1.5\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$ relative to the rope. Find the magnitude of the block's acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Let the block accelerate up at $a$; then the rope on the monkey's side moves down at $a$, so the monkey's ground acceleration is $a_{rel} - a$. Equal masses feel the same tension, so $T - mg = m(a_{rel}-a)$ and $T - mg = ma$. Therefore $a = a_{rel}/2 = 0.75\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$: both rise, at the same rate.

name: Hooke's law force
statement: A spring with stiffness $k = 250\;\mathrm{N/m}$ is stretched $0.12\;\mathrm{m}$ from its natural length. Find the magnitude of the force it exerts, in newtons.
solution: Hooke's law gives $F = kx = (250)(0.12) = 30\;\mathrm{N}$, directed back toward the natural length.

name: Finding k from a hanging mass
statement: Hanging a $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass from a spring stretches it by $0.080\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the spring constant, in $\mathrm{N/m}$.
solution: At equilibrium $kx = mg$, so $k = (2.0)(9.8)/0.080 = 245\;\mathrm{N/m}$.

name: Equilibrium extension
statement: A $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass hangs from a spring with $k = 400\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Find the extension at equilibrium, in meters.
solution: Setting $kx = mg$ gives $x = 49/400 = 0.1225\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Springs in parallel
statement: Two springs of stiffness $200\;\mathrm{N/m}$ and $300\;\mathrm{N/m}$ are attached side by side between a block and a wall, so both stretch by the same amount. Find the effective spring constant, in $\mathrm{N/m}$.
solution: Equal stretch means the forces add: $F = (k_1+k_2)x$. So $k_{eff} = 200+300 = 500\;\mathrm{N/m}$.

name: Springs in series
statement: The same two springs ($200\;\mathrm{N/m}$ and $300\;\mathrm{N/m}$) are instead joined end to end. Find the effective spring constant of the combination, in $\mathrm{N/m}$.
solution: In series both springs carry the same force and the extensions add, so $1/k_{eff} = 1/200 + 1/300$. That gives $k_{eff} = 120\;\mathrm{N/m}$, softer than either spring.

name: Energy stored in a spring
statement: A spring with $k = 800\;\mathrm{N/m}$ is compressed by $0.050\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the elastic potential energy stored, in joules.
solution: The stored energy is $U = \tfrac12kx^2 = \tfrac12(800)(0.0025) = 1.0\;\mathrm{J}$.

name: Force at a given stretch
statement: A bungee trainer uses a spring of stiffness $150\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Find the force needed to hold it stretched $0.20\;\mathrm{m}$, in newtons.

name: Period of a spring-block system
statement: A $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless surface is attached to a spring of stiffness $100\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Find the period of oscillation, in seconds.
solution: The period is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.040} = 1.26\;\mathrm{s}$.

name: Oscillation frequency
statement: A $0.50\;\mathrm{kg}$ glider on an air track is attached to a spring with $k = 200\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Find the oscillation frequency, in hertz.
solution: Here $\omega = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{400} = 20\;\mathrm{rad/s}$, so $f = \omega/2\pi = 3.18\;\mathrm{Hz}$.

name: Two springs in series holding a load
statement: A $6.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass hangs from two identical springs of stiffness $300\;\mathrm{N/m}$ joined end to end. Find the total extension, in meters.
solution: In series the pair behaves as one spring of $k_{eff} = 150\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Then $x = mg/k_{eff} = 58.8/150 = 0.392\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Cutting a spring in half
statement: A spring of stiffness $240\;\mathrm{N/m}$ is cut exactly in half, and a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass is hung from one of the halves. Find the extension, in meters.
solution: Each coil of the original spring stretched the same amount, so half the spring stretches half as much under the same force: the half-spring has $k = 480\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Then $x = 29.4/480 = 0.0613\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Period from the static sag
statement: A mass hung from a vertical spring stretches it by $0.050\;\mathrm{m}$ at equilibrium. Find the period of small vertical oscillations, in seconds.
solution: Since $k = mg/x_0$, the period $2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ becomes $2\pi\sqrt{x_0/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.0051} = 0.449\;\mathrm{s}$. The mass itself drops out.

name: Maximum speed of an oscillator
statement: A $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless floor is attached to a spring with $k = 500\;\mathrm{N/m}$, pulled $0.10\;\mathrm{m}$ from equilibrium, and released. Find its maximum speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: All the stored energy becomes kinetic at the equilibrium point: $\tfrac12kA^2 = \tfrac12mv^2$, so $v = A\sqrt{k/m} = 0.10(15.81) = 1.58\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Spring gun
statement: A toy gun uses a spring with $k = 900\;\mathrm{N/m}$ compressed by $0.060\;\mathrm{m}$ to launch a $0.050\;\mathrm{kg}$ ball horizontally. Find the launch speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: The spring energy $\tfrac12kx^2 = 1.62\;\mathrm{J}$ all goes to the ball: $v = x\sqrt{k/m} = 0.060\sqrt{18000} = 8.05\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Block between two springs
statement: A $1.2\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless floor is connected to opposite walls by springs of stiffness $100\;\mathrm{N/m}$ and $200\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Find the frequency of oscillation, in hertz.
solution: Displacing the block stretches one spring and compresses the other, and both push it back, so the constants add: $k_{eff} = 300\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Then $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{300/1.2} = 2.52\;\mathrm{Hz}$.

name: Spring on an incline
statement: A $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block rests on a frictionless $25^\circ$ incline, held by a spring of stiffness $400\;\mathrm{N/m}$ running along the incline. Find the spring's extension, in meters.
solution: Along the incline the spring balances $mg\sin\theta = 12.4\;\mathrm{N}$, so $x = 12.4/400 = 0.0311\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Spring in an accelerating elevator
statement: A $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass hangs from a spring of stiffness $600\;\mathrm{N/m}$ inside an elevator accelerating upward at $2.5\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the spring's extension, in meters.
solution: The spring must both support the weight and provide the acceleration: $kx = m(g+a)$. So $x = 4.0(12.3)/600 = 0.082\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Series pair under load
statement: Springs of stiffness $100\;\mathrm{N/m}$ and $400\;\mathrm{N/m}$ are joined end to end and a $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass is hung from the pair. Find the total extension, in meters.
solution: The series combination has $k_{eff} = (100)(400)/500 = 80\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Then $x = 19.6/80 = 0.245\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Spring constant from a period
statement: A $0.25\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass on a spring oscillates with a period of $0.60\;\mathrm{s}$. Find the spring constant, in $\mathrm{N/m}$.
solution: Invert $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ to get $k = 4\pi^2m/T^2 = 4\pi^2(0.25)/0.36 = 27.4\;\mathrm{N/m}$.

name: Spring between two accelerating blocks
statement: A $1.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block and a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless floor are joined by a spring. A horizontal force of $8.0\;\mathrm{N}$ pushes the $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block toward the other, and the spring settles at a fixed compression. Find the force the spring exerts, in newtons.
solution: Once the compression is steady both blocks share the acceleration $a = 8.0/4.0 = 2.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The spring is the only horizontal force on the $1.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block, so it pushes with $2.0\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Work done stretching a spring
statement: A spring requires a $45\;\mathrm{N}$ force to hold it stretched $0.15\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the work needed to stretch it that far from its natural length, in joules.
solution: The force grows linearly, so the work is the area of a triangle: $W = \tfrac12Fx = \tfrac12(45)(0.15) = 3.375\;\mathrm{J}$. Using $F = kx$ with $k = 300\;\mathrm{N/m}$ gives the same.

name: Scaling the load
statement: A $1.5\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass hung from a spring stretches it $0.060\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the extension when a $4.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass hangs from the same spring, in meters.
solution: Extension is proportional to load, so $x = 0.060(4.0/1.5) = 0.16\;\mathrm{m}$. (The spring constant is $k = 245\;\mathrm{N/m}$ if you prefer to compute it.)

name: Mass released on a spring
statement: A $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block is attached to a vertical spring of stiffness $400\;\mathrm{N/m}$, held so the spring is at its natural length, and released from rest. Find the maximum extension reached, in meters.
solution: Energy conservation gives $mgx = \tfrac12kx^2$, so $x = 2mg/k = 0.098\;\mathrm{m}$. That is twice the equilibrium sag, because the block overshoots and oscillates about equilibrium.

name: Dropped onto a spring
statement: A $1.5\;\mathrm{kg}$ block is dropped from rest $0.30\;\mathrm{m}$ above the top of a vertical spring of stiffness $1200\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Find the maximum compression of the spring, in meters.
solution: At maximum compression $x$ the block is momentarily at rest, so $mg(h+x) = \tfrac12kx^2$. This gives $600x^2 - 14.7x - 4.41 = 0$, whose positive root is $x = 0.0989\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Two springs stacked vertically
statement: A $5.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass hangs from a spring of stiffness $300\;\mathrm{N/m}$, which itself hangs from a spring of stiffness $200\;\mathrm{N/m}$ attached to the ceiling. Find the total extension of the pair, in meters.
solution: Both springs carry the same $49\;\mathrm{N}$, and the extensions add: $x = 49(1/300 + 1/200) = 0.408\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Slipping on an oscillating block
statement: A $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block rides on top of a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block attached to a spring of stiffness $200\;\mathrm{N/m}$, and the pair oscillates horizontally. The coefficient of static friction between the blocks is $0.40$. Find the largest amplitude for which the top block does not slide, in meters.
solution: The peak acceleration of the oscillation is $\omega^2A$ with $\omega^2 = k/M_{total} = 40\;\mathrm{s^{-2}}$. Friction can only supply $\mu_s g = 3.92\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, so $A_{max} = 3.92/40 = 0.098\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Spring pushing two free blocks apart
statement: A compressed spring of stiffness $800\;\mathrm{N/m}$ is held between a $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block and a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block on a frictionless floor, compressed $0.050\;\mathrm{m}$. The blocks are released and the spring falls away. Find the final speed of the $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Momentum starts at zero, so $2v_2 = 3v_3$. Energy gives $\tfrac12(800)(0.0025) = 1.0\;\mathrm{J}$ shared as kinetic energy. Solving, the relative speed is $\sqrt{2(1.0)/1.2} = 1.29\;\mathrm{m/s}$ and the $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block takes the larger share: $v = 0.775\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Cut into three, joined in parallel
statement: A spring of stiffness $120\;\mathrm{N/m}$ is cut into three equal pieces, and the three pieces are attached side by side to a $0.50\;\mathrm{kg}$ block so that they all stretch together. Find the oscillation frequency, in hertz.
solution: Each third has stiffness $3k = 360\;\mathrm{N/m}$, and three in parallel give $9k = 1080\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Then $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{1080/0.50} = 7.40\;\mathrm{Hz}$.

name: Instant after the string is cut
statement: A $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hangs from a spring attached to the ceiling, and a $3.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block hangs from the first block by a string. The string is cut. Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ block immediately afterward, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: A spring's length cannot change instantly, so right after the cut it still pulls up with $(2.0+3.0)g = 49\;\mathrm{N}$. The upper block now weighs only $19.6\;\mathrm{N}$, so its net upward force is $29.4\;\mathrm{N}$ and $a = 29.4/2.0 = 14.7\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$ upward.

name: Mass on a movable pulley and spring
statement: One end of a spring with $k = 800\;\mathrm{N/m}$ is fixed to the ceiling; the other end passes around a movable pulley that carries a $2.0\;\mathrm{kg}$ mass, and the rope's far end is also tied to the ceiling. Find the period of small vertical oscillations of the mass, in seconds.
solution: If the mass drops by $x$, both supporting segments lengthen by $x$, so the spring stretches $2x$ and its tension is $2kx$. The mass hangs on two segments, so the restoring force is $2(2kx) = 4kx$: the effective stiffness is $4k = 3200\;\mathrm{N/m}$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{2.0/3200} = 0.157\;\mathrm{s}$.

name: Centripetal force on a whirling ball
statement: A $0.50\;\mathrm{kg}$ ball moves in a horizontal circle of radius $1.2\;\mathrm{m}$ at $4.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the centripetal force on it, in newtons.
solution: $F = mv^2/r = (0.50)(16)/1.2 = 6.67\;\mathrm{N}$, directed toward the center.

name: Centripetal acceleration of a car
statement: A car takes a curve of radius $25\;\mathrm{m}$ at $10\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find its centripetal acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Speed from period
statement: A stone on a string travels a circle of radius $0.80\;\mathrm{m}$, completing one revolution every $2.0\;\mathrm{s}$. Find its speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: One revolution covers $2\pi r = 5.03\;\mathrm{m}$ in $2.0\;\mathrm{s}$, so $v = 2.51\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Record player
statement: A point on a record $0.15\;\mathrm{m}$ from the center spins at $45\;\mathrm{rev/min}$. Find its centripetal acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: First convert: $\omega = 45(2\pi)/60 = 4.71\;\mathrm{rad/s}$. Then $a_c = \omega^2r = (4.71)^2(0.15) = 3.33\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Force on a cornering car
statement: A $1000\;\mathrm{kg}$ car rounds a curve of radius $50\;\mathrm{m}$ at $15\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the centripetal force required, in newtons.
solution: $F = mv^2/r = (1000)(225)/50 = 4500\;\mathrm{N}$, supplied by friction from the road.

name: Bottom of a vertical circle
statement: A $0.20\;\mathrm{kg}$ ball on a $0.50\;\mathrm{m}$ string swings in a vertical circle and passes the lowest point at $5.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the string tension there, in newtons.
solution: At the bottom the tension pulls up and gravity pulls down, and the net must point up (toward the center): $T - mg = mv^2/r$. So $T = 0.20(50+9.8) = 12.0\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Minimum speed at the top
statement: A ball on a string of length $0.80\;\mathrm{m}$ is swung in a vertical circle. Find the minimum speed at the top for the string to stay taut, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: At the critical speed the string goes slack and gravity alone supplies the centripetal force: $mg = mv^2/r$, so $v = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{7.84} = 2.8\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Swinging a bucket of water
statement: A bucket of water is swung in a vertical circle of radius $1.0\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the minimum speed at the top for the water to stay in, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: The water stays in as long as the bucket bottom does not need to pull it inward. The limit is when gravity alone provides $v^2/r$: $v = \sqrt{gr} = 3.13\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Centrifuge
statement: A sample sits $0.10\;\mathrm{m}$ from the axis of a centrifuge spinning at $100\;\mathrm{rad/s}$. Find its centripetal acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Child on a merry-go-round
statement: A $25\;\mathrm{kg}$ child sits $2.0\;\mathrm{m}$ from the axis of a merry-go-round that turns once every $6.0\;\mathrm{s}$. Find the horizontal force needed to hold the child in the circle, in newtons.

name: Tension at the top
statement: A $0.30\;\mathrm{kg}$ ball on a $0.60\;\mathrm{m}$ string passes the top of a vertical circle at $4.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the string tension there, in newtons.
solution: At the top both tension and gravity point toward the center: $T + mg = mv^2/r$. So $T = 0.30(26.67-9.8) = 5.06\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Loop-the-loop release height
statement: A small cart starts from rest on a frictionless track and runs through a vertical loop of radius $3.0\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the minimum starting height above the bottom of the loop, in meters.
solution: At the top the cart needs $v^2 = gR$. Energy conservation gives $gh = g(2R) + \tfrac12v^2 = 2gR + \tfrac12gR$, so $h = 2.5R = 7.5\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Crest of a hill
statement: A car drives over a hill whose crest has radius of curvature $40\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the speed at which the car just barely loses contact with the road, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Contact is lost when the normal force reaches zero and gravity alone bends the path: $g = v^2/r$, so $v = \sqrt{(9.8)(40)} = 19.8\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Normal force at the crest
statement: A $1200\;\mathrm{kg}$ car crosses the crest of a hill of radius $40\;\mathrm{m}$ at $15\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the normal force from the road, in newtons.
solution: Toward the center (downward) $mg - N = mv^2/r$, so $N = m(g - v^2/r) = 1200(9.8-5.625) = 5010\;\mathrm{N}$, well below the car's weight.

name: Rotor ride
statement: In a rotor ride, riders stand against the inside wall of a cylinder of radius $3.0\;\mathrm{m}$ and the floor drops away. The coefficient of static friction is $0.40$. Find the minimum wall speed for riders to stay up, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: The wall's normal force supplies the centripetal force $mv^2/r$, and friction $\mu_sN$ must support the weight. Combining, $\mu_s mv^2/r \ge mg$, so $v \ge \sqrt{gr/\mu_s} = \sqrt{73.5} = 8.57\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Coin on a turntable
statement: A coin lies $0.12\;\mathrm{m}$ from the axis of a turntable, with $\mu_s = 0.30$. Find the maximum angular speed before the coin slides, in $\mathrm{rad/s}$.
solution: Friction supplies the centripetal force: $\mu_smg \ge m\omega^2r$. So $\omega_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_sg/r} = \sqrt{24.5} = 4.95\;\mathrm{rad/s}$.

name: Pendulum released from horizontal
statement: A $0.40\;\mathrm{kg}$ ball on a string is released from rest with the string horizontal. Find the string tension as the ball passes the lowest point, in newtons.
solution: Energy gives $v^2 = 2gL$ at the bottom. Then $T - mg = mv^2/L = 2mg$, so $T = 3mg = 11.8\;\mathrm{N}$: three times the weight, whatever the length.

name: Speed at the equator
statement: Earth has radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$ and turns once per $86400\;\mathrm{s}$. Find the speed of a point on the equator, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Centripetal acceleration at the equator
statement: Using the same Earth data, find the centripetal acceleration of a point on the equator, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: $a_c = v^2/R = (463)^2/(6.37\times 10^6) = 0.0337\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. This is why the measured $g$ at the equator is slightly less than at the poles.

name: String breaking point
statement: A $0.80\;\mathrm{kg}$ ball is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius $1.5\;\mathrm{m}$ on a string that snaps at $60\;\mathrm{N}$. Find the maximum speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Setting $mv^2/r = T_{max}$, $v = \sqrt{T_{max}r/m} = \sqrt{112.5} = 10.6\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Top to bottom of a vertical circle
statement: A ball on a $1.2\;\mathrm{m}$ string passes the top of a vertical circle at $5.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find its speed at the bottom, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: The drop from top to bottom is $2r = 2.4\;\mathrm{m}$, and the string does no work. Energy gives $v_b^2 = v_t^2 + 4gr = 25+47.04$, so $v_b = 8.49\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Pilot at the bottom of a loop
statement: A pilot of mass $75\;\mathrm{kg}$ flies through the bottom of a vertical loop of radius $500\;\mathrm{m}$ at $100\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the force of the seat on the pilot, in newtons.
solution: At the bottom $N - mg = mv^2/r$, so $N = 75(9.8+20.0) = 2235\;\mathrm{N}$, about three times the pilot's weight.

name: Tension at the bottom for the critical loop
statement: A $0.25\;\mathrm{kg}$ ball is swung in a vertical circle at exactly the minimum speed at the top. Find the string tension at the lowest point, in newtons.
solution: At the top $v_t^2 = gr$; energy then gives $v_b^2 = gr + 4gr = 5gr$. At the bottom $T = mg + mv_b^2/r = mg + 5mg = 6mg = 14.7\;\mathrm{N}$, independent of the radius.

name: Leaving a spherical dome
statement: A small block slides from rest at the top of a frictionless dome of radius $1.5\;\mathrm{m}$. Find its height above the center of the dome at the moment it leaves the surface, in meters.
solution: While in contact, $mg\cos\theta - N = mv^2/R$, and energy gives $v^2 = 2gR(1-\cos\theta)$. Setting $N = 0$ gives $\cos\theta = 2/3$, so the height above the center is $R\cos\theta = 1.0\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Rigid rod instead of a string
statement: A ball on the end of a light rigid rod of length $0.70\;\mathrm{m}$ is balanced at the top of a vertical circle and given a tiny nudge. Find its speed at the bottom, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: A rod can push as well as pull, so the ball may start with essentially zero speed at the top. Falling a height $2L$ gives $v = \sqrt{4gL} = \sqrt{27.44} = 5.24\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Friction budget while cornering
statement: A car travels at $20\;\mathrm{m/s}$ around a flat curve of radius $100\;\mathrm{m}$ on a road with $\mu_s = 0.80$. Find the maximum additional braking deceleration available without skidding, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Total friction is limited to $\mu_sg = 7.84\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and turning already uses $v^2/r = 4.0\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$ of it. The remaining component is perpendicular: $\sqrt{7.84^2-4.0^2} = 6.74\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Two beads on one rotating string
statement: Two $0.30\;\mathrm{kg}$ beads are fixed on a light string rotating in a horizontal circle about one end at $5.0\;\mathrm{rad/s}$: one at $0.40\;\mathrm{m}$ and one at $0.80\;\mathrm{m}$ from the axis. Find the tension in the inner segment, in newtons.
solution: The inner segment must supply the centripetal force for both beads: $T = m\omega^2r_1 + m\omega^2r_2 = 3.0+6.0 = 9.0\;\mathrm{N}$. The outer segment carries only $6.0\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Ferris wheel at the top
statement: A Ferris wheel of radius $15\;\mathrm{m}$ turns once every $40\;\mathrm{s}$. Find the force of the seat on a $60\;\mathrm{kg}$ rider at the top, in newtons.
solution: The centripetal acceleration is $4\pi^2r/T^2 = 0.370\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, pointing down at the top. So $mg - N = ma_c$ gives $N = 60(9.8-0.370) = 566\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Tension in a rotating chain
statement: A uniform chain of mass $0.20\;\mathrm{kg}$ and length $0.50\;\mathrm{m}$ is whirled in a horizontal circle about one end at $10\;\mathrm{rad/s}$. Find the tension at the midpoint of the chain, in newtons.
solution: Integrate the centripetal requirement of every element beyond the cut: $T(x) = \int_x^L (m/L)\omega^2 s\,ds = \frac{m\omega^2}{2L}(L^2-x^2)$. At $x = 0.25\;\mathrm{m}$ this gives $T = (0.20)(100)(0.1875)/1.0 = 3.75\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Bead in a rotating hoop
statement: A bead slides without friction on a circular hoop of radius $0.40\;\mathrm{m}$ that spins about a vertical diameter at $8.0\;\mathrm{rad/s}$. Find the angle from the bottom of the hoop at which the bead sits in steady equilibrium, in degrees.
solution: The bead circles at radius $R\sin\theta$, so the normal force from the hoop must satisfy $N\sin\theta = m\omega^2R\sin\theta$ horizontally and $N\cos\theta = mg$ vertically. Dividing gives $\cos\theta = g/(\omega^2R) = 9.8/25.6 = 0.383$, so $\theta = 67.5^\circ$.

name: Design angle for a curve
statement: A curve of radius $80\;\mathrm{m}$ is to be banked so that a car at $20\;\mathrm{m/s}$ needs no friction. Find the bank angle, in degrees.
solution: For frictionless banking, $\tan\theta = v^2/(gr) = 400/784 = 0.510$. So $\theta = 27.0^\circ$.

name: Design speed of a bank
statement: A curve of radius $120\;\mathrm{m}$ is banked at $15^\circ$. Find the speed at which no friction is needed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: From $\tan\theta = v^2/(gr)$, $v = \sqrt{gr\tan\theta} = \sqrt{(9.8)(120)(0.268)} = 17.7\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Conical pendulum period
statement: A conical pendulum of length $1.2\;\mathrm{m}$ swings with its string $25^\circ$ from the vertical. Find the period, in seconds.
solution: The period of a conical pendulum is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\theta/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{1.088/9.8} = 2.09\;\mathrm{s}$.

name: Tension in a conical pendulum
statement: A $0.40\;\mathrm{kg}$ ball swings as a conical pendulum with the string $30^\circ$ from the vertical. Find the string tension, in newtons.
solution: The vertical component of tension balances gravity: $T\cos\theta = mg$, so $T = 3.92/\cos 30^\circ = 4.53\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Speed of a conical pendulum
statement: A conical pendulum has a string of length $0.80\;\mathrm{m}$ making $40^\circ$ with the vertical. Find the ball's speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: The circle radius is $r = L\sin\theta = 0.514\;\mathrm{m}$, and dividing the horizontal and vertical equations gives $v^2 = gr\tan\theta = 4.23$. So $v = 2.06\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Frictionless banked turn
statement: A curve of radius $60\;\mathrm{m}$ is banked at $20^\circ$ and the surface is icy (no friction). Find the only speed at which a car can hold the curve, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: $v = \sqrt{gr\tan\theta} = \sqrt{(9.8)(60)(0.364)} = 14.6\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Faster and it slides up the bank, slower and it slides down.

name: Airplane in a banked turn
statement: An airplane flying at $150\;\mathrm{m/s}$ banks at $30^\circ$ so that the lift force, perpendicular to the wings, turns it. Find the radius of the turn, in meters.
solution: Lift plays the role of the normal force, so the same relation applies: $r = v^2/(g\tan\theta) = 22500/5.66 = 3980\;\mathrm{m}$.

name: Radius from design speed
statement: A highway ramp banked at $15^\circ$ is designed for $25\;\mathrm{m/s}$ with no reliance on friction. Find the radius of the ramp, in meters.

name: Normal force on a banked curve
statement: A $1500\;\mathrm{kg}$ car takes a $20^\circ$ banked curve at exactly the design speed, so friction is zero. Find the normal force from the road, in newtons.
solution: Vertically $N\cos\theta = mg$, so $N = 14700/\cos 20^\circ = 1.56\times 10^4\;\mathrm{N}$, larger than the car's weight.

name: Angular speed of a conical pendulum
statement: A conical pendulum of length $0.50\;\mathrm{m}$ hangs $60^\circ$ from the vertical. Find its angular speed, in $\mathrm{rad/s}$.
solution: From $\omega^2 = g/(L\cos\theta)$, $\omega = \sqrt{9.8/0.25} = 6.26\;\mathrm{rad/s}$.

name: Maximum speed with friction
statement: A curve of radius $50\;\mathrm{m}$ is banked at $10^\circ$, with $\mu_s = 0.30$. Find the maximum safe speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: At maximum speed friction points down the bank. Combining the two force equations gives $v_{max} = \sqrt{gr\frac{\tan\theta+\mu}{1-\mu\tan\theta}} = \sqrt{246} = 15.7\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Minimum speed with friction
statement: A curve of radius $50\;\mathrm{m}$ is banked steeply at $25^\circ$, with $\mu_s = 0.20$. Find the minimum speed at which a car can hold the curve without sliding down the bank, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Now friction points up the bank, flipping the signs: $v_{min} = \sqrt{gr\frac{\tan\theta-\mu}{1+\mu\tan\theta}} = \sqrt{119} = 10.9\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Friction on a slow car
statement: A $1200\;\mathrm{kg}$ car creeps at $10\;\mathrm{m/s}$ around a curve of radius $70\;\mathrm{m}$ banked at $18^\circ$. Find the friction force on the car along the surface, in newtons.
solution: The car is slower than the design speed, so friction must act up the slope. Resolving along the surface, $f = m(g\sin\theta - \frac{v^2}{r}\cos\theta) = 1200(3.03-1.36) = 2.00\times 10^3\;\mathrm{N}$.

name: Longer conical pendulum
statement: A conical pendulum of length $2.0\;\mathrm{m}$ makes an angle of $15^\circ$ with the vertical. Find its period, in seconds.
solution: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\theta/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{1.932/9.8} = 2.79\;\mathrm{s}$. For small angles this is nearly the ordinary pendulum period.

name: Cone angle from the period
statement: A conical pendulum of length $0.90\;\mathrm{m}$ completes one revolution every $1.50\;\mathrm{s}$. Find the angle of the string from the vertical, in degrees.
solution: Rearranging $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\theta/g}$ gives $\cos\theta = gT^2/(4\pi^2L) = 22.05/35.53 = 0.621$, so $\theta = 51.6^\circ$.

name: Banking a railway curve
statement: A railway curve of radius $300\;\mathrm{m}$ is to be banked for trains traveling at $30\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the required bank angle, in degrees.

name: Motorcycle lean angle
statement: A motorcyclist rounds a flat curve of radius $40\;\mathrm{m}$ at $18\;\mathrm{m/s}$, leaning so the total force from the ground passes through the rider's center of mass. Find the lean angle from the vertical, in degrees.
solution: The ground force must have vertical component $mg$ and horizontal component $mv^2/r$, so $\tan\theta = v^2/(gr) = 324/392 = 0.827$ and $\theta = 39.6^\circ$: the same formula as a bank angle.

name: Conical pendulum from the radius
statement: A ball on a $1.0\;\mathrm{m}$ string moves in a horizontal circle of radius $0.60\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the ball's speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Here $\sin\theta = 0.60$ so $\cos\theta = 0.80$ and $\tan\theta = 0.75$. Then $v = \sqrt{gr\tan\theta} = \sqrt{4.41} = 2.1\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Mass does not matter
statement: A frictionless curve of radius $45\;\mathrm{m}$ is banked at $30^\circ$. Find the design speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: $v = \sqrt{gr\tan\theta} = \sqrt{(9.8)(45)(0.577)} = 16.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Notice the mass cancels, so a loaded truck and a small car have the same design speed.

name: Load factor in a bank
statement: A pilot puts an aircraft into a level $50^\circ$ banked turn. Find the ratio of the lift force to the aircraft's weight.
solution: Vertical balance requires $L\cos\theta = mg$, so $L/mg = 1/\cos 50^\circ = 1.56$. The pilot feels $1.56$ times normal weight.

name: Revolutions per minute
statement: A conical pendulum of length $0.60\;\mathrm{m}$ hangs $35^\circ$ from the vertical. Find its rotation rate, in revolutions per minute.
solution: First $\omega = \sqrt{g/(L\cos\theta)} = \sqrt{9.8/0.491} = 4.47\;\mathrm{rad/s}$. Converting, $(4.47)(60)/(2\pi) = 42.6\;\mathrm{rev/min}$.

name: Parked on a bank
statement: A car is parked on a frictionless curve banked at $30^\circ$ and released from rest. Find the magnitude of its initial acceleration, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: At rest there is no centripetal requirement, so the bank is just a frictionless incline: $a = g\sin 30^\circ = 4.9\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$ down the slope.

name: Racing on a shallow bank
statement: A track of radius $90\;\mathrm{m}$ is banked at $12^\circ$, with $\mu_s = 0.50$. Find the maximum speed a car can carry through it, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Use $v_{max} = \sqrt{gr\frac{\tan\theta+\mu}{1-\mu\tan\theta}}$. With $\tan 12^\circ = 0.213$, this is $\sqrt{882(0.713)/0.894} = \sqrt{703} = 26.5\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Friction required at high speed
statement: A curve of radius $150\;\mathrm{m}$ is banked at $15^\circ$ and a car takes it at $30\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the minimum coefficient of static friction needed.
solution: Write $v^2/(gr) = 0.612$ and invert the maximum-speed formula: $\mu = \frac{v^2/(gr)-\tan\theta}{1+(v^2/(gr))\tan\theta} = 0.344/1.164 = 0.296$.

name: Steep conical pendulum
statement: A conical pendulum of length $1.0\;\mathrm{m}$ swings with the string $60^\circ$ from the vertical. Find the ball's speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: With $r = L\sin\theta$, $v^2 = gL\sin\theta\tan\theta = (9.8)(0.866)(1.732) = 14.7$. So $v = 3.83\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Slowest safe speed on a steep bank
statement: A bobsled run of radius $60\;\mathrm{m}$ is banked at $35^\circ$, with $\mu_s = 0.25$. Find the minimum speed to avoid sliding down the bank, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Friction acts up the bank at the minimum speed: $v_{min} = \sqrt{gr\frac{\tan\theta-\mu}{1+\mu\tan\theta}} = \sqrt{588(0.450)/1.175} = 15.0\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Period is set by the angle alone
statement: Two conical pendulums of length $1.5\;\mathrm{m}$ carry balls of $0.20\;\mathrm{kg}$ and $0.80\;\mathrm{kg}$, and both are observed to hang $20^\circ$ from the vertical. Find their common period, in seconds.
solution: The mass cancels from both force equations, so the period depends only on $L$ and $\theta$: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\theta/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{1.410/9.8} = 2.38\;\mathrm{s}$.

name: Puck inside a smooth funnel
statement: A puck slides in a horizontal circle of radius $0.60\;\mathrm{m}$ on the smooth inside surface of a funnel whose wall makes $40^\circ$ with the horizontal. Find the puck's speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: The normal force is perpendicular to the wall, so it has an upward component $N\sin\theta = mg$ and an inward component $N\cos\theta = mv^2/r$. Dividing gives $v^2 = gr/\tan\theta = 7.01$, so $v = 2.65\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Note this is the reciprocal of the road-banking relation, because the surface tilts the other way.

name: Very steep bank, very high grip
statement: A test track section of radius $50\;\mathrm{m}$ is banked at $45^\circ$, with $\mu_s = 0.90$. Find the maximum speed the track can support, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Here $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, so $v_{max} = \sqrt{gr\frac{1+\mu}{1-\mu}} = \sqrt{490(1.9)/0.1} = 96.5\;\mathrm{m/s}$. The denominator $1-\mu\tan\theta$ is nearly zero, which is why the answer blows up: at $\mu\tan\theta = 1$ there is no maximum speed at all.

name: String at its breaking tension
statement: A $0.60\;\mathrm{kg}$ ball on a $1.2\;\mathrm{m}$ string is swung as a conical pendulum. The string breaks at $20\;\mathrm{N}$. Find the greatest speed the ball can have, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: The vertical equation $T\cos\theta = mg$ fixes the angle at breaking: $\cos\theta = 5.88/20 = 0.294$, so $\sin\theta = 0.956$ and $\tan\theta = 3.25$. Then $v = \sqrt{gL\sin\theta\tan\theta} = \sqrt{36.6} = 6.05\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Earth pulling the Moon
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. The Moon has mass $7.35\times 10^{22}\;\mathrm{kg}$, Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$, and the centers are $3.84\times 10^8\;\mathrm{m}$ apart. Find the gravitational force between Earth and Moon, in newtons.

name: Surface gravity from mass and radius
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the gravitational field strength at Earth's surface, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: $g = GM/R^2 = (6.67\times 10^{-11})(5.97\times 10^{24})/(6.37\times 10^6)^2 = 9.81\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, matching the measured value.

name: Two people attracting
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. Two $100\;\mathrm{kg}$ people stand with their centers $2.0\;\mathrm{m}$ apart. Find the gravitational force between them, in newtons.
solution: $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2 = (6.67\times 10^{-11})(10^4)/4 = 1.67\times 10^{-7}\;\mathrm{N}$, far too small to notice.

name: Orbital speed in low Earth orbit
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the orbital speed of a satellite $400\;\mathrm{km}$ above the surface, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ with $r = 6.77\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. That gives $v = 7.67\times 10^3\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Escape speed from Earth
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the escape speed from Earth's surface, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Setting total energy to zero, $\tfrac12mv^2 = GMm/R$, so $v = \sqrt{2GM/R} = 1.12\times 10^4\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Field at twice the radius
statement: The gravitational field at Earth's surface is $9.81\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the field strength at a point two Earth radii from Earth's center, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: The field falls off as $1/r^2$, so doubling the distance divides it by four: $9.81/4 = 2.45\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Weight at high altitude
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the gravitational force on a $70\;\mathrm{kg}$ astronaut $1000\;\mathrm{km}$ above Earth's surface, in newtons.
solution: Here $r = 7.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$, so $g = GM/r^2 = 7.33\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and $F = (70)(7.33) = 513\;\mathrm{N}$. Astronauts are not beyond gravity's reach.

name: Period of a low orbit
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. A satellite orbits $400\;\mathrm{km}$ above the surface. Find its orbital period, in seconds.
solution: With $r = 6.77\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$ and $v = 7671\;\mathrm{m/s}$, the period is $T = 2\pi r/v = 5.54\times 10^3\;\mathrm{s}$, about 92 minutes.

name: Surface gravity of the Moon
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. The Moon has mass $7.35\times 10^{22}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and radius $1.74\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find its surface gravity, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: $g = GM/R^2 = (6.67\times 10^{-11})(7.35\times 10^{22})/(1.74\times 10^6)^2 = 1.62\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, about one sixth of Earth's.

name: Force on an orbiting satellite
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the gravitational force on a $500\;\mathrm{kg}$ satellite whose orbit radius is $8.0\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$, in newtons.

name: Geostationary radius
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. A satellite is to orbit with a period of $86164\;\mathrm{s}$ so that it stays above one spot on the equator. Find its orbital radius, in meters.
solution: Set $GMm/r^2 = m4\pi^2r/T^2$ and solve: $r = (GMT^2/4\pi^2)^{1/3} = 4.22\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$, roughly $6.6$ Earth radii.

name: Escape speed from the Moon
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. The Moon has mass $7.35\times 10^{22}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and radius $1.74\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the escape speed from its surface, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Neutral point between Earth and Moon
statement: The Earth ($5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$) and Moon ($7.35\times 10^{22}\;\mathrm{kg}$) have centers $3.84\times 10^8\;\mathrm{m}$ apart. Find the distance from Earth's center to the point on the line between them where the net gravitational field is zero, in meters.
solution: Setting $GM_E/x^2 = GM_M/(d-x)^2$ gives $x/(d-x) = \sqrt{M_E/M_M} = 9.01$. So $x = d/(1+\sqrt{M_M/M_E}) = 3.46\times 10^8\;\mathrm{m}$, about 90% of the way to the Moon.

name: Period at two Earth radii
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the period of a circular orbit of radius $1.274\times 10^7\;\mathrm{m}$ (two Earth radii), in seconds.
solution: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM} = 2\pi\sqrt{(2.068\times 10^{21})/(3.983\times 10^{14})} = 1.43\times 10^4\;\mathrm{s}$, just under four hours.

name: Gravity inside the Earth
statement: Model Earth as a uniform sphere with surface gravity $9.81\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the gravitational field at a depth of half an Earth radius, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Only the mass inside your radius matters, and for a uniform sphere that gives $g \propto r$. At $r = R/2$ the field is half the surface value: $4.90\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Energy to raise a satellite
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the work needed to move a $1000\;\mathrm{kg}$ payload from Earth's surface to a point two Earth radii from the center (ignore kinetic energy), in joules.
solution: Using $U = -GMm/r$, the change is $GMm(1/R - 1/2R) = GMm/(2R) = (3.983\times 10^{14})(1000)/(1.274\times 10^7) = 3.13\times 10^{10}\;\mathrm{J}$.

name: Speed of the Moon
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. The Moon orbits at a radius of $3.84\times 10^8\;\mathrm{m}$. Find its orbital speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Weighing the Sun
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. Earth orbits the Sun at a radius of $1.496\times 10^{11}\;\mathrm{m}$ with a period of $3.156\times 10^7\;\mathrm{s}$. Find the Sun's mass, in kilograms.

name: A bigger, less dense planet
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. A planet has twice Earth's mass ($5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$) and twice Earth's radius ($6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$). Find its surface gravity, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Since $g = GM/R^2$, doubling $M$ doubles $g$ but doubling $R$ divides it by four. The net is half of Earth's value: $4.90\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Mean density of Earth
statement: Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find Earth's mean density, in $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
solution: $\rho = M/(\tfrac43\pi R^3) = (5.97\times 10^{24})/(1.083\times 10^{21}) = 5.51\times 10^3\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, roughly twice the density of surface rock.

name: Total energy of an orbit
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. An $800\;\mathrm{kg}$ satellite is in a circular orbit of radius $7.0\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the magnitude of its total mechanical energy, in joules.
solution: For a circular orbit the kinetic energy is $GMm/2r$ and the potential energy is $-GMm/r$, so $E = -GMm/2r$. The magnitude is $(3.983\times 10^{14})(800)/(1.4\times 10^7) = 2.28\times 10^{10}\;\mathrm{J}$.

name: Launch speed to reach one Earth radius up
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the launch speed needed for a projectile to just reach a height of one Earth radius above the surface (ignore air and rotation), in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Energy conservation gives $\tfrac12v^2 = GM(1/R - 1/2R) = GM/2R$, so $v = \sqrt{GM/R} = 7.91\times 10^3\;\mathrm{m/s}$. That is exactly the low-orbit speed, and $1/\sqrt2$ of escape speed.

name: Tunnel through the Earth
statement: A straight tunnel is bored through the center of a uniform Earth (surface gravity $9.81\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$, radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$) and an object is dropped in. Find the period of the resulting oscillation, in seconds.
solution: Inside a uniform sphere the field is $g r/R$, a restoring force proportional to displacement, so the motion is simple harmonic with $\omega^2 = g/R$. Then $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R/g} = 5.06\times 10^3\;\mathrm{s}$, about 84 minutes: the same as a low orbit.

name: Binary star period
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. Two stars of mass $2.0\times 10^{30}\;\mathrm{kg}$ each orbit their common center of mass, with a separation of $1.0\times 10^{12}\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the orbital period, in seconds.
solution: Each star circles at radius $d/2$ with the full separation setting the force: $GM^2/d^2 = M4\pi^2(d/2)/T^2$. This rearranges to $T = 2\pi\sqrt{d^3/(G(M_1+M_2))} = 3.85\times 10^8\;\mathrm{s}$.

name: Change in g with altitude
statement: Earth has radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$ and surface gravity $9.81\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Find the decrease in $g$ at an altitude of $10\;\mathrm{km}$, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: For $h \ll R$, $g(h) \approx g(1-2h/R)$, so $\Delta g \approx 2gh/R = 2(9.81)(10^4)/(6.37\times 10^6) = 0.0308\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. A commercial airliner's altitude changes weight by only about $0.3\%$.

name: Extra speed to escape from orbit
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. A satellite is in a circular orbit of radius $7.0\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Find the additional speed it must gain to escape Earth entirely, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Circular speed is $\sqrt{GM/r} = 7545\;\mathrm{m/s}$ and escape speed at the same radius is $\sqrt2$ times that, $10670\;\mathrm{m/s}$. The difference is $3.13\times 10^3\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Field off the axis of two masses
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. Two $1.00\times 10^3\;\mathrm{kg}$ spheres sit $2.00\;\mathrm{m}$ apart. Find the magnitude of the gravitational field at a point $1.00\;\mathrm{m}$ from the midpoint, on the perpendicular bisector, in $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
solution: Each sphere is $\sqrt2\;\mathrm{m}$ away, contributing $GM/r^2 = 3.34\times 10^{-8}\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The components along the bisector add and the perpendicular ones cancel, so the total is $2(3.34\times 10^{-8})\cos 45^\circ = 4.72\times 10^{-8}\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

name: Leaving the solar system
statement: Earth orbits the Sun at $2.978\times 10^4\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Ignoring Earth's own gravity, find the speed a probe at Earth's orbital radius needs to escape the Sun, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: For a circular orbit the escape speed at that radius is $\sqrt2$ times the orbital speed, since $v_{esc}^2 = 2GM/r = 2v_{circ}^2$. So $v = \sqrt2(2.978\times 10^4) = 4.21\times 10^4\;\mathrm{m/s}$.

name: Falling from two Earth radii
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. An object is released from rest at a distance of two Earth radii from Earth's center. Find its speed on reaching the surface (ignore the atmosphere), in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Energy conservation with the correct $1/r$ potential gives $\tfrac12v^2 = GM(1/R - 1/2R) = GM/2R$. Then $v = \sqrt{GM/R} = 7.91\times 10^3\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Using a constant $g$ over that distance would be badly wrong.

name: Speeding up as a satellite decays
statement: Use $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and Earth's mass is $5.97\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius $6.37\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$. Atmospheric drag lowers a satellite's circular orbit from $300\;\mathrm{km}$ to $200\;\mathrm{km}$ altitude. Find the increase in its orbital speed, in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
solution: Orbital speed is $\sqrt{GM/r}$, so it grows as the orbit shrinks: $7784$ vs $7726\;\mathrm{m/s}$, an increase of $58\;\mathrm{m/s}$. Drag removes energy yet the satellite ends up moving faster, because the potential energy drops by twice as much as the kinetic energy gains.

name: Third law with AU and years
statement: An asteroid orbits the Sun with a semi-major axis of $4.00\;\mathrm{AU}$. Find its orbital period, in years.
solution: In these units Kepler's third law is simply $T^2 = a^3$. So $T = 4^{3/2} = 8.00\;\mathrm{years}$.

name: Working backward to the radius
statement: A comet orbits the Sun with a period of $27.0\;\mathrm{years}$. Find its semi-major axis, in AU.

name: Period of Mars
statement: Mars orbits the Sun with a semi-major axis of $1.524\;\mathrm{AU}$. Find its orbital period, in years.
solution: $T = a^{3/2} = 1.524^{3/2} = 1.881\;\mathrm{years}$, close to the observed value of about 687 days.

name: Distance of Jupiter
statement: Jupiter takes $11.86\;\mathrm{years}$ to orbit the Sun. Find its semi-major axis, in AU.

name: Doubling the orbit radius
statement: Satellite B orbits Earth in a circle of exactly twice the radius of satellite A's orbit. Find the ratio of B's period to A's period.
solution: Since $T \propto a^{3/2}$, the ratio is $2^{3/2} = 2.83$.

name: Four times the radius
statement: A satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius $r$ to one of radius $4r$. Find the factor by which its period increases.
